title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a data-sourcing decision made before deployment. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified specific sources including YouTube, Deezer, and Genius. That training produced a system capable of generating outputs that closely reproduce protected works, including distinctive vocal characteristics and melodic elements, when prompted with details about decade, genre, and artist style. The failure sits at the training stage, not in any single output: the capacity to reproduce copyrighted material was baked in before any user made a request.

The lawsuits were brought by major labels, independent artists through class actions, the German collecting society GEMA, and a music publisher, across multiple jurisdictions. A German court found against Suno on copyright grounds. Warner Music Group reached a settlement with Suno, and Universal Music settled with Udio, while other litigation remains active. A musicians' union subsequently filed suit against the labels themselves over those settlement deals. What is not established is whether any court in the United States has issued a final verdict on the copyright infringement claims against either company.

Catching this kind of failure would have required auditing training data for licensed status before ingestion, or building filtering mechanisms capable of detecting memorized reproduction at inference time. Neither step was reported to have been taken. The labels' demonstration, using targeted prompts to repeatedly elicit near-copies of specific recordings, suggests that reproduction of protected material was not an edge case but a reproducible behavior of the deployed system.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, and Warner Music have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno, alleging the companies scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their systems. The labels claim the AI services not only illegally used massive amounts of music but also directly reproduce sections of famous songs by artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Chuck Berry, and Mariah Carey. The companies have refused to disclose their training data and previously argued their use constitutes fair use.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly recreate famous copyrighted songs by using targeted prompts that specified details like decade, genre, and artist style. For example, specific prompts generated outputs closely mimicking Green Day's American Idiot and Mariah Carey's holiday hit, even reproducing distinctive vocal characteristics and melodic elements. The labels submitted thousands of examples and a thumb drive of AI-generated music as evidence. The lawsuits also target unnamed individuals who allegedly helped the companies scrape music, setting up a significant legal battle over how generative AI can train on copyrighted material.
